From the third of June, a new bus will run to the airport. The number is seventy-two. Buses leave every fifteen minutes from Bridge Street. A single ticket costs four pounds fifty.

The swimming club meets on Thursday evenings at seven o'clock. New members must bring a towel and a photo. The coach is Mr Brennan, B, R, E, N, N, A, N. The first lesson is free, and after that it costs six pounds.
The weekend market moves to Park Road next month. There will be thirty stalls selling fruit, bread and cheese. It opens at nine a.m. and closes at two p.m.

The health centre has a new phone number. It is oh one six one, four nine eight, two two seven three. The centre is closed on Sunday. To see a nurse, arrive before ten o'clock. The new doctor is Dr Patel, P, A, T, E, L. Parking costs two pounds.

A cooking course starts on the twelfth of October. There are eight lessons, one each week. The course costs ninety-six pounds. Students learn to make Italian pasta and French desserts. Classes are in Room B four.
Museum tours now start at eleven a.m. Each tour lasts about ninety minutes. Children under five go free. Adults pay seven pounds. Please meet the guide at the main entrance.
You can now rent a bike near the station. It costs three pounds an hour or fifteen pounds for a full day. You need to show a passport or driving licence. The shop closes at six p.m.

The careers fair takes place on the twenty-first of March at the Hilton Hotel. More than sixty companies will attend. Entry is free, but you must register online by the eighteenth. The organiser, Mr Gorman, G, O, R, M, A, N, advises students to bring ten copies of their CV.

A new survey shows that thirty-eight per cent of workers in the city now cycle to work. Ten years ago the figure was only twelve per cent. The council plans to build twenty-five kilometres of new bike lanes by twenty twenty-eight. The project will cost four point two million pounds.

The new student flats on Carlton Avenue will be ready in September. Each flat has six bedrooms and a shared kitchen. Rent is a hundred and fifteen pounds a week, including bills. Applications close on the thirtieth of June.

This year's music festival runs for three days, from Friday the ninth of August. Over forty bands will play on four stages. A weekend ticket costs eighty-five pounds, and camping is twenty pounds extra.

Repairs on the main road will begin at ten p.m. on Tuesday. The road will be closed for five nights. Drivers should use Mill Lane instead. Buses number fourteen and 22 will also change their route. For details, call oh eight hundred, three one two, five five six.

The book club meets on the first Wednesday of every month in the café on Grove Street. This month's book is about a journey across Canada. The meeting starts at six forty-five. Members pay two pounds fifty for coffee and cake.

Tomorrow will be sunny in the morning, with temperatures reaching twenty-four degrees. In the afternoon, strong winds are expected along the coast. Rain will arrive on Saturday night. Next week, temperatures will fall to around sixteen degrees, which is four degrees below average.

The city park needs volunteers to plant five hundred trees on the fourteenth of November. Volunteers should arrive at nine fifteen and wear strong boots. Lunch is provided. To sign up, email Ms Okafor, O, K, A, F, O, R.

Researchers at the university studied two thousand four hundred teenagers. They found that students who slept less than seven hours scored eighteen per cent lower in maths tests. The lead researcher, Professor Lindqvist, L, I, N, D, Q, V, I, S, T, recommends that schools start classes after nine a.m.

The airport will open a third terminal in twenty thirty-one. It will handle twelve million passengers a year. The project costs about nine hundred million pounds, and it will create three and a half thousand jobs. Local residents are worried about noise.

Small businesses in the region grew by six point five per cent last year, the fastest rate since twenty fifteen. Most growth came from online retail. However, one in four owners said finding skilled staff was their biggest problem. The report was published on the second of May.

Your booking reference is K, T, seven, three, nine, two. You have reserved a double room for four nights, arriving on the twenty-sixth of July. The total price is four hundred and thirty-six pounds. Check-in is from three p.m.

Solar power now produces fourteen per cent of the country's electricity, up from just two per cent a decade ago. The government aims to reach forty per cent by twenty forty. The biggest solar farm is near the town of Ashford, A, S, H, F, O, R, D.

The exchange programme sends a hundred and twenty students abroad every year. Students spend five months at a partner university, usually in Japan or Australia. The grant covers flights and up to six hundred and fifty pounds a month for living costs. The deadline is the first of February.

The national park welcomed one point eight million visitors last year. To protect wildlife, the number of cars will be limited to three hundred a day from April. Visitors are encouraged to take the shuttle bus, which costs five pounds return.

A survey of eight hundred and fifty adult learners found that sixty-four per cent study a language on their phones. The most popular time to practise is between nine and ten in the evening. The most studied language after English is Spanish. The survey was carried out in December.

A single ticket costs four pounds for adults. Mr Garrod, that's G, A, R, R, O, D, the harbour manager, says extra boats will sail at weekends from the eighteenth of this month.

The Westmoor Farmers' Fair opens on Wednesday at ten thirty in the town square. Entry is free, but cheese and jam cost two pounds a jar. The organiser, Ms Quennell, that's Q, U, E, N, N, E, L, L, says there will be a cooking show at lunchtime. Around twenty-four local farms will sell fresh vegetables, honey and eggs. Parking is free behind the church.

Our next story is about the Riverside Charity Run. The race starts on Sunday at eight o'clock from the sports centre. Entry costs fifteen pounds, and all money goes to a children's hospital. Ms Fenwick, that's F, E, N, W, I, C, K, the event leader, says runners must register before the thirtieth. Water stations will be placed every two kilometres along the route.

The Fitness Point gym on Park Road has a special offer for students. From Monday, membership costs twenty pounds a month instead of forty-five pounds. The manager, Mr Ruddock, that's R, U, D, D, O, C, K, says new members can also book three free trial classes. The offer ends on the first of next month. Ask at the front desk for details.

The Greenfield Zoo has some exciting news for families. A baby elephant was born on Thursday. Visitors can see it from ten o'clock next week. Entry costs seven pounds for adults. Dr Dunmore, that's D, U, N, M, O, R, E, the head keeper, says the baby weighs ninety kilos. The zoo will also open four new penguin pools in spring.

Commuters on the Eastline should expect delays this week. Trains will be cancelled on Friday because of track repairs. The earliest service will now leave at seven fifteen. Ms Hollis, that's H, O, L, L, I, S, the station spokesperson, says delays can last up to forty-five minutes. Repairs should finish by the third, so check the website before you travel.

The Lakeview Camera Club is holding a photography contest. Photos must be sent in by twelve thirty on Saturday. The first prize is fifty pounds, and the judge, Mr Ashdown, that's A, S, H, D, O, W, N, has won many awards. Each person may enter up to twenty-five pictures. Winners will be announced at the town hall next month.

The Central High School science fair opens to the public on Thursday. Visitors can arrive at nine forty-five, and entry is free. Dr Thackray, that's T, H, A, C, K, R, A, Y, the fair organiser, says there will be sixteen projects about robots and plants. The awards ceremony will take place on the second of June.

The Northgate Community Garden is looking for new members. Sign-up day is this Sunday, from eight thirty in the morning. Membership costs ten pounds a year, which covers tools and seeds. Ms Ogilvie, that's O, G, I, L, V, I, E, the garden leader, says there are thirty-five empty plots left. Anyone over twelve can join. Please bring your own gloves.

Drivers in Oak Lane should note new parking rules from Friday. Cars cannot park on the street between seven o'clock and nine o'clock in the morning. Ms Kimber, that's K, I, M, B, E, R, from the council, says the fine for breaking the rule is sixty pounds. New signs will be put up by the end of the week. Residents with a permit can still park there.

The Hillside Animal Shelter needs help this week. Adoption events will be held on Wednesday, between eleven thirty and three o'clock. Ms Sorrell, that's S, O, R, R, E, L, L, says a dog named Biscuit will be ready for a new home. Adoption fees are twenty-five pounds, which covers vaccines. The shelter has room for eighteen more cats.

The Corn Exchange Theatre opens a new play this month. The show called The Long Road starts on Friday at seven thirty in the evening. Tickets cost eighteen pounds for the best seats. The director, Dr Hartwell, that's H, A, R, T, W, E, L, L, says the cast has practised for six months. Booking closes on the twenty-first.

A new coffee shop called Bean Street will open on Thursday at eight o'clock. A cup of coffee will cost three pounds during the first week. Owner Mr Penrose, that's P, E, N, R, O, S, E, says the first fifty customers will receive a free muffin. The shop is near the bus station on Market Road. It also sells tea and cakes.

Electricity will be switched off in the Brookfield area on Tuesday. The power cut starts at six o'clock in the evening and lasts for four hours. Mr Mabbott, that's M, A, B, B, O, T, T, the site engineer, says the work is needed to repair a broken cable. Customers who need medical equipment should call the helpline. The repair should finish by the twelfth.

Smart Phone Repairs, a shop on Canal Street, has a special offer this weekend. Screen repairs will cost thirty pounds for all phones. Owner Mr Wragg, that's W, R, A, G, G, says most jobs take only two days. The shop is open on Saturday until five o'clock in the evening. Customers can also get a free phone case.

Riverside Driving School is offering free taster lessons for new drivers. The first session starts on Tuesday at ten fifteen in the morning. Instructor Ms Pascoe, that's P, A, S, C, O, E, says a normal lesson costs thirty-five pounds. Students must be at least eighteen years old to sign up. Places are limited to the first thirty people.

The Carlton Youth Orchestra will give a free concert on Sunday at two o'clock in the church hall. Conductor Mr Lowther, that's L, O, W, T, H, E, R, says the group has forty young musicians this year. The concert includes music from famous films. Donations are welcome, and the money will buy new instruments. Auditions for next year will take place on the fourteenth.

A beach clean-up will take place at Sandy Cove. The event starts on Saturday at nine thirty in the morning. Ms Corrigan, that's C, O, R, R, I, G, A, N, from the local charity, says organisers hope to collect sixty bags of rubbish. Gloves and bags will be provided for everyone. The next clean-up is planned for the third.

The Central Adult Learning Centre has a new computer course for beginners. Classes start on Monday at six thirty in the evening. The tutor, Dr Threlfall, that's T, H, R, E, L, F, A, L, L, says students will learn to use email and spreadsheets. The course costs forty pounds for the full term. Each class has a maximum of ten learners.

A new dance class for teenagers will begin at the community centre on Thursday. Sessions run from seven o'clock until eight o'clock each week. Teacher Ms Ormerod, that's O, R, M, E, R, O, D, says no experience is needed. Each session costs six pounds, but the first week is free. Booking for the course closes on the fifth.

Parents can now book places at the Summer School Holiday Camp. The camp runs every weekday, starting on Monday at nine o'clock in the morning. Camp leader Ms Hewson, that's H, E, W, S, O, N, says children will do sports, art and science. A full week costs forty-five pounds. There are only twelve places left. Lunch is included.

The lost property office at Central Station will close at four thirty on Wednesday for staff training. Supervisor Mr Brannigan, that's B, R, A, N, N, I, G, A, N, says items can still be collected by post. A small fee of five pounds applies to postal collection. Items not collected within twenty-eight days will be given to charity. Please bring proof of ownership when you visit.

A new riverside walking path will open to the public on Friday. The first guided walk leaves at eight fifteen in the morning from the bridge. Mr Mottram, that's M, O, T, T, R, A, M, the park ranger, says the path is five kilometres long. Walkers should wear comfortable shoes. The official opening ceremony will be held on the eleventh.

Central Post Office on High Street will close for repairs from Tuesday. Customers can use a mobile van, which parks outside the church from nine thirty each morning. Postmaster Ms Lanyon, that's L, A, N, Y, O, N, says the building should reopen by the seventeenth. Stamps can still be bought for eight pounds from local shops. The nearest branch is two miles away.

The regional blood service is holding a donation drive at the Civic Hall, which opens on the twenty-first of March. Organiser Mr Pargeter, P, A, R, G, E, T, E, R, says the hall needs four hundred new donors every week. Sessions run until seven forty-five in the evening, and every donor receives a voucher worth four pounds fifty. Last year, the number of donors rose by fifteen per cent.

Work on the new tram line between the railway station and Harbour Road is due to finish by the third of June. The transport department expects it to carry one thousand two hundred passengers a day, with single fares set at one pound eighty. Councillor Ms Dunstan, D, U, N, S, T, A, N, says the line will cut traffic on Mill Street. Trams are due to start at six fifteen in the morning.

The annual film festival opens next Friday at the Regent Cinema, with more than eighty films from fourteen countries. Festival director Dr Coverdale, C, O, V, E, R, D, A, L, E, says tickets go on sale at nine thirty tomorrow morning. A ticket for the opening night costs twelve pounds, and students get a discount of twenty percent. All screenings take place in the Ellis Room.

The university will hold its open day on the fourteenth of September, when more than two thousand five hundred visitors are expected. Admissions tutor Ms Haskett, H, A, S, K, E, T, T, says free shuttle buses run from the station from ten thirty onwards. The event runs all day and includes talks, tours and free refreshments. Parking is limited, so please use the car park.

Applications are now open for the city's job training scheme, which starts on the fifth of May. There are sixty places on the course, and each trainee receives a weekly allowance. Programme manager Ms Vosper, V, O, S, P, E, R, says a deposit of three hundred fifty pounds is refunded once the course is complete. Last year, eighty-five per cent of trainees found work within six months.

Tickets are selling fast for the charity concert at the Old Town Hall, which takes place on the eighteenth of October. The venue has four hundred fifty seats, and the doors open at eight o'clock in the evening. Organiser Mr Ashdown, A, S, H, D, O, W, N, says that a standard ticket costs twenty-five pounds, and all proceeds go to the children's hospice. Please book early.

The Environment Agency has issued a flood warning for low-lying areas along the River Lea after heavy rain. A spokesman, Mr Tremlett, T, R, E, M, L, E, T, T, says river levels could rise by forty-five centimetres. Residents should expect water on local roads by six thirty tonight. Sandbags are available from the fire station. Forecasters say there is a seventy per cent chance of more rain this weekend.

Average house prices in the town rose by three per cent over the last three months, according to a survey published this morning. Economist Dr Lathbury, L, A, T, H, B, U, R, Y, says the typical home now costs two hundred and twelve thousand pounds. An earlier estimate suggested prices had fallen, but that was corrected. The main reason is the shortage of rented flats. The next figures are due on the fifteenth of December.

Parking charges at the General Hospital will change from the first of April. The number of spaces for disabled drivers will increase to forty bays. Hospital director Ms Quennell, Q, U, E, N, N, E, L, L, says the changes will pay for a new multi-storey building. Work starts at nine o'clock on Monday morning. Visitors arriving by bus can still use the free drop-off zone, which will stay open twenty-four hours a day.

The Riverside Sports Centre will close for refurbishment on the sixteenth of February, and it will stay shut for six weeks. The centre currently has one thousand eight hundred members, and all memberships will be extended for one month. Councillor Mr Brackley, B, R, A, C, K, L, E, Y, says the work will include a new gym and an upgraded pool. The pool reopens at ten thirty on Saturday. The main upgrade is to the changing rooms.

The town's food bank is asking for donations before the eighth of December. Last month it helped three hundred and fifty families. Volunteer coordinator Ms Penhale, P, E, N, H, A, L, E, says the most needed items are tinned fish, rice and cooking oil. A donation of five pounds pays for a week of meals. Every bag makes a real difference. Drop off your donations at the community centre.

The council says it has missed its recycling target for the second year running. Only twenty-seven per cent of household waste was recycled last year, against a target of forty per cent. Cabinet member Mr Sheldrake, S, H, E, L, D, R, A, K, E, says residents should use the new brown bins. A new collection timetable starts on the first of March. Collections will begin at seven o'clock in the morning.

Entries are now open for the city's startup competition for young entrepreneurs. The winner will receive ten thousand pounds in funding, and an earlier notice giving a lower figure has been corrected. Judges include businesswoman Ms Wakefield, W, A, K, E, F, I, E, L, D, and two local investors. The deadline for applications is the twenty-eighth of February. Each team can have up to five members. Finalists will pitch their ideas in the town hall.

The Lantern Theatre Festival begins on the twelfth of July. Over three thousand tickets have already been sold. Festival co-founder Dr Rendell, R, E, N, D, E, L, L, says the programme includes twenty new plays. The opening show starts at seven thirty in the evening. Tickets for the closing night are available from the box office. The final performance takes place in the rooftop garden, weather permitting.

The Science Museum's new planetarium opens to the public on the thirtieth of August. Tickets for the first show cost eight pounds fifty. Curator Ms Tallis, T, A, L, L, I, S, says the dome seats up to one hundred twenty visitors at once. The shows will focus on the night sky and the planets of our solar system. Morning sessions start at eleven fifteen, and booking is strongly recommended.

Work on the new cycling lane along Canal Road will finish on the nineteenth of May. Councillor Dr Hollings, H, O, L, L, I, N, G, S, says the lane will be three metres wide, which allows cyclists to pass safely. Officials hope it will reduce accidents. Cyclists can use the route from six forty-five each morning. The project also includes new traffic lights at the junction with Station Street.

The council has approved a budget of forty-eight million pounds for next year. Leader of the council, Ms Mellor, M, E, L, L, O, R, says the largest share will go to road repairs. Libraries will receive three point five million pounds, while council tax will rise by four per cent. Residents can read the full figures online. The new budget takes effect on the second of April.

Applications for the summer internship programme close on the twenty-third of January. Local firms are offering sixty-four paid places across the region. Programme coordinator Mr Yarwood, Y, A, R, W, O, O, D, says the scheme is open to all second-year students. Interviews take place from nine fifteen each weekday. The programme lasts ten weeks. Students should bring a copy of their transcript to every meeting.

The school board has confirmed a new uniform policy, which will apply from the start of September term. Head teacher Dr Kettering, K, E, T, T, E, R, I, N, G, says the cost of a school blazer will fall by twenty per cent. A sweatshirt will cost no more than fifteen pounds. Pupils must arrive at the gate by eight forty every morning. Parents with questions should contact the school office.

The candidates for the Westfield council seat will take part in a public debate on the seventeenth of October at the community hall. Candidate Ms Whitlock, W, H, I, T, L, O, C, K, has confirmed her attendance. Tickets are free, but there are only one hundred eighty seats available. Doors open at six forty-five, and the debate will be broadcast online. A survey suggests that thirty-eight per cent of voters are still undecided.

Residents are invited to join the town's free fitness challenge, which begins on the first of June. Participants must walk or run at least ten thousand steps each day. Organiser Mr Garrod, G, A, R, R, O, D, says the scheme is open to people of all ages. Registration closes at five o'clock on the Friday before the start. Prizes include a free gym membership for the winner.

Water bills will rise by six per cent from the start of next year, the water company has confirmed. Customer services manager Ms Pendry, P, E, N, D, R, Y, says the increase is needed to repair old pipes. A typical household will pay around four hundred twenty pounds a year. The company plans to replace one thousand five hundred kilometres of pipes. Customers can check their bills by calling the helpline.

The first night market of the season opens in Harbour Square on the fourth. More than sixty stalls will sell food, crafts and clothing. Organiser Ms Ormerod, O, R, M, E, R, O, D, says stalls open from five thirty until midnight. Most stalls accept cards, so visitors should not bring large amounts of cash. Live music will be played on the main stage, and entry is free.

Engineers have completed the new footbridge over the river at Eastgate, and it will open to pedestrians on the ninth of May. The bridge is forty-five metres long. Project lead Dr Sowerby, S, O, W, E, R, B, Y, says the design was chosen after a public vote. The cost of the project was two point one million pounds. Cyclists may cross as well, but e-scooters are not allowed on the bridge.

Residents should not be alarmed by sirens on the eleventh of October, because the council is running an emergency drill. The exercise involves about two hundred people, including police, paramedics and firefighters. Planning officer Mr Ellerby, E, L, L, E, R, B, Y, says sirens will sound at ten o'clock, and the drill will last about an hour. Drivers should avoid the town centre and use the ring road instead.

Applications are open for a free coding bootcamp run by the Digital Skills Centre. The course lasts twelve weeks and places are limited to twenty-four students. Course tutor Ms Gatling, G, A, T, L, I, N, G, says the first session starts at six o'clock in the evening. No previous experience is needed, and lunch is provided. Students will need their own laptop to take part.

Volunteers are needed for this year's wildlife count, which takes place on the twenty-second of March. Experts will lead twelve guided walks across the reserve. Local naturalist Mr Fennimore, F, E, N, N, I, M, O, R, E, says last year's count recorded over forty species of birds. Children are welcome with an adult. Participants should arrive at the visitor centre by eight thirty. Please bring binoculars and a notebook.

A heritage walk through the old quarter will be led by local historian Dr Dunmore, D, U, N, M, O, R, E. The route takes about ninety minutes and includes the medieval church and the old canal wharf. The walks start from the Market Cross. Tickets for the evening walk cost six pounds, although children go free. Wear comfortable shoes. Walks run every Sunday in June.

A team of hydrologists led by Professor Lindqvist, L, I, N, D, Q, V, I, S, T, has measured plastic particles in the Rhône River. Water samples were taken from forty-two sites between the Alps and the delta, and almost every sample contained microplastics. At the busiest sites, the team counted roughly two thousand four hundred particles per cubic metre. Earlier surveys had reported nine hundred, but the new figures come from a method called spectroscopy, which detects fragments as small as ten micrometres. The authors estimate that about eighteen per cent of the particles originate from washing synthetic clothing, and that the contaminated stretch extends for forty kilometres below the city of Lyon.

Scientists at a research station in Kenya, led by Dr Okonkwo, O, K, O, N, K, W, O, report that wild bee numbers on highland farms have fallen steeply since the early nineteen eighties. Their latest survey estimates that the region now supports only one point five million wild bees, far below the two million that earlier studies had suggested. The team links the decline to a group of pesticides called neonicotinoids. Farms that stopped using them recorded a rise of eighteen per cent in bee visits within two seasons.

A materials laboratory in Finland, headed by Professor Brandvold, B, R, A, N, D, V, O, L, D, has tested a new lithium battery designed for electric cars. The prototype retains ninety-two per cent of its capacity after two thousand charging cycles, a clear improvement on today's cells. The design replaces cobalt with a cathode based on manganese, a cheaper and more widely available metal. Engineers predict that commercial production could begin by twenty thirty-one, although earlier forecasts placed the date at twenty twenty-seven. Early vehicles could travel up to six hundred kilometres on a single charge.

Glaciologists working in Norway, under the direction of Dr Halvorsen, H, A, L, V, O, R, S, E, N, report that the Jostedal glacier lost one point two million cubic metres of ice last summer, the largest annual loss since measurements began in nineteen sixty-two. Satellite images show that the ice front has retreated by four hundred metres since the start of the century. Earlier models had predicted a smaller loss, and the team now says the glacier has shrunk by eighteen per cent in volume since the mid-century. Next spring, the team will drill ice cores to test their models.

Archaeologists from a university in Romania, led by Professor Teodorescu, T, E, O, D, O, R, E, S, C, U, have uncovered a bronze age settlement near the Danube. Radar surveys suggest that the site covers about one hundred and forty hectares, which would make it one of the largest settlements of its era in the region. Excavations since twenty fourteen have revealed a defensive wall built from mudbrick and storage pits containing roughly one thousand two hundred fragments of pottery. Earlier maps had shown only a few dozen mounds on the site, which suggests that the settlement was buried by river sediment for centuries.

A sleep clinic in South Africa has published results from a trial led by Dr Mbatha, M, B, A, T, H, A, involving three hundred and twelve adults aged between sixty and eighty. Volunteers who slept for at least seven hours scored eighteen per cent higher on memory tests than those who slept less. Earlier studies had suggested that the effect was small, but the researchers believe that deep sleep supports a process called consolidation, in which new memories move into long-term storage. The trial began in twenty nineteen and will continue for two more years.

Oceanographers at an institute in Chennai, led by Dr Varghese, V, A, R, G, H, E, S, E, report that the surface waters of the Bay of Bengal have warmed by zero point eight degrees between nineteen eighty-five and twenty twenty-five. The team links the change to a weakening of the layering known as stratification, which traps heat near the surface. Satellite estimates had suggested only half a degree, but moored buoys show the number of marine heatwaves has grown by twelve per cent since two thousand.

Agronomists at a university in the Philippines, led by Professor Kowalczyk, K, O, W, A, L, C, Z, Y, K, have tested a new rice variety in paddy fields across three provinces. The variety yielded an average of seven point four tonnes per hectare, compared with about five point nine tonnes in conventional fields. Field trials began in twenty sixteen, and the gain comes from a gene that helps plants tolerate salinity, a growing problem in coastal deltas. The team estimates that seeds could be planted on two point five million hectares within a decade, although the figure depends on government approval.

A child development study from the Netherlands, directed by Dr Osterhaus, O, S, T, E, R, H, A, U, S, followed four thousand eight hundred children for three years. Those who spent more than four hours a day on screens were thirty-four per cent more likely to show poor attention in class. Parents often assumed that educational apps were harmless, though the researchers found the effect was similar for games. The strongest link appeared with multitasking, which the authors define as switching tasks every few minutes. The full dataset will be released in twenty twenty-eight.

Engineers at a North Sea energy consortium, coordinated by Dr Abendroth, A, B, E, N, D, R, O, T, H, say their new offshore turbine array generated one point nine terawatt hours of electricity during its first year, enough to supply roughly four hundred and fifty thousand households. Early plans had forecast a lower output of one point two terawatt hours, but the turbines were placed further offshore where winds are stronger. Maintenance costs remain high, and performance is still affected by turbulence at the turbine blades. Engineers also reported that the array's capacity factor reached forty-one per cent, well above the national average.

Marine biologists from a research vessel expedition, led by Professor Castellano, C, A, S, T, E, L, L, A, N, O, have identified sixty-three previously unknown animals at depths of more than four thousand metres in the Atacama Trench. Many of the creatures survive on detritus, organic matter that sinks from the upper ocean. Earlier expeditions, the last of which took place in nineteen ninety-five, had suggested that the trench held only about forty species, but the new count indicates it may hold more than one thousand one hundred species.

Microbiologists at a hospital network in Bulgaria, led by Dr Dimitrov, D, I, M, I, T, R, O, V, have tracked resistance to a common antibiotic in urinary infections across one hundred and twenty wards over five years. The proportion of resistant samples rose from nine per cent to twenty-seven per cent by twenty twenty-four. Earlier reports had suggested the figure was stable, but the team found that most resistance spread through plasmids, small rings of DNA that carry resistance genes between bacteria. A prescribing policy introduced in twenty nineteen reduced the number of antibiotic courses by a fifth, though the effect has weakened since.

A cardiology team in Japan, directed by Professor Sundquist, S, U, N, D, Q, U, I, S, T, followed six thousand two hundred adults over a period of twelve years. Participants who drank at least three cups of green tea a day had a twenty-two per cent lower risk of heart failure. The researchers stressed that tea alone does not prevent disease, and earlier trials had produced mixed results. The protective effect appeared to depend on the level of polyphenols in the drink, a group of plant compounds. The cohort was recruited in nineteen ninety-eight, and the findings were published this month.

Atmospheric scientists at a research centre in Canada, led by Dr Pellegrin, P, E, L, L, E, G, R, I, N, found that smoke from forest fires in the summer of twenty twenty-one reached cities nearly four thousand kilometres away. Monitoring stations recorded fine particle levels of one hundred and eighty micrograms per cubic metre, nearly six times the guideline. Hospitals reported a rise in asthma admissions, although earlier models had predicted a smaller effect. The team relied on a simulation of atmospheric transport to trace the smoke's path across the continent.

Researchers at an engineering school in Japan, led by Dr Nakashima, N, A, K, A, S, H, I, M, A, say that recovering metals from discarded phones could meet eighteen per cent of the country's annual demand for gold. Their pilot plant processed one point two million handsets last year. Earlier estimates had put the recoverable share at thirty per cent, but the team's process, which relies on leaching, recovers far more metal from circuit boards. The plant will open in twenty twenty-seven at an industrial site near Osaka.

A water engineering group in Israel, supervised by Professor Ruzicka, R, U, Z, I, C, K, A, has trialled a greenhouse system that grows tomatoes using brackish water and sunlight alone. Over two growing seasons, the greenhouses produced three thousand six hundred kilograms of tomatoes per hectare, which is about sixty per cent of the yield from irrigated fields in the valley. The system relies on condensation from night air, which feeds a storage tank holding fifteen thousand litres. Earlier projects in the region had failed because of high salt levels, but the new design avoids that problem.

Ornithologists at a Finnish field station, led by Dr Vuorinen, V, U, O, R, I, N, E, N, have fitted one thousand seven hundred barn swallows with tiny GPS tags. The birds travel from Finland to southern Africa each autumn, covering about nine thousand kilometres in roughly three weeks. Earlier studies had estimated that the journey took six weeks, but the tags show that many birds stop at wetlands along the Nile for several days. The team found that the proportion of birds returning to the same nest fell by twenty-three per cent after the drought of twenty twenty-two.

Acoustic engineers at a university in Iran, led by Dr Haddadi, H, A, D, D, A, D, I, measured traffic noise in sixty city districts over one year. Night-time levels exceeded the recommended limit in almost all areas, and residents near motorways reported insomnia. Earlier surveys had put the average at fifty-five decibels, but the team's sensors recorded values around seventy decibels during the evening rush. A quieter road surface reduced the noise by eight decibels in the trial streets.

A labour economics study at a university in Scotland, directed by Professor Gallacher, G, A, L, L, A, C, H, E, R, tracked three thousand one hundred employees at a software firm across two years of hybrid working. Output per worker rose by eleven per cent during the first year, though it fell back to baseline in the second. The authors argue that the gains came from autonomy over working hours rather than from reduced commuting. Managers who judged staff by hours, not results, saw smaller gains. The firm's hybrid policy was first introduced in twenty twenty-one and remains in place.

Civil engineers at a construction firm in Nigeria, managed by Dr Oyelaran, O, Y, E, L, A, R, A, N, report that a three D printing machine built a single-storey house covering forty-six square metres in thirty-eight hours of printing time. The concrete mixture uses local clay and recycled glass, which lowers the cost by twenty-two per cent compared with conventional brick. Earlier printed buildings relied on steel reinforcement, which the team has replaced with a polymer mesh that holds the walls together.

Environmental health researchers in Portugal, led by Professor Ferreira, F, E, R, R, E, I, R, A, measured carbon dioxide levels in one hundred and eighty classrooms during winter lessons. In more than half of them, concentrations rose above one thousand parts per million, a level linked to drowsiness. Opening windows reduced the peak by thirty-five per cent, but many schools lack mechanical ventilation. Earlier guidance had suggested that a single open window was enough. The team recommends installing sensors that alert teachers when air quality drops.

Astronomers at an observatory in India, led by Dr Pradhan, P, R, A, D, H, A, N, have catalogued twenty-seven thousand pieces of debris larger than ten centimetres in low Earth orbit. Collisions between old satellites and rocket stages are responsible for most of the fragments, and the number has grown by forty per cent since twenty twenty. Earlier agencies had counted only about twenty thousand objects, but the team's radar data suggest a cascade of collisions could make parts of orbit unusable by twenty fifty.

Volcanologists at an observatory in Indonesia, under the leadership of Dr Kanamaru, K, A, N, A, M, A, R, U, installed forty-five seismometers and gas sensors on the slopes of a volcano that last erupted in nineteen ninety-four. Over six months, the network detected ground swelling of twelve centimetres around the crater, along with a rise in sulphur dioxide. Earlier models had linked the signal to rainfall, but the team's analysis suggests that magma is moving through a conduit beneath the summit. Authorities have asked two thousand three hundred people living within the danger zone to prepare for evacuation.

Biochemists at a laboratory in Brazil, led by Professor Benkhedda, B, E, N, K, H, E, D, D, A, have engineered a bacterium that breaks down PET plastic at thirty degrees Celsius, which is much lower than the temperatures needed by earlier enzymes. In laboratory tests the bacterium removed ninety-six per cent of a plastic film within one hundred and twenty hours. Early versions had produced toxic by-products, but the team's modified strain converts the plastic into acetate, a compound used in industry.

A psychology team at a school of education in Denmark, led by Dr Eskildsen, E, S, K, I, L, D, S, E, N, tested whether daily music lessons improve reading. Among five hundred and forty pupils aged seven and eight, those who took part in rhythm training scored fourteen per cent higher on phonological tests after one year. The authors argue that the benefit comes from improved attention rather than from musical skill itself. Teachers in the control group reported no comparable change. The programme was first piloted in two thousand nine.

Nutrition scientists at a university in Quebec, led by Dr Tremblay, T, R, E, M, B, L, A, Y, followed nine thousand adults for eight years. Those who consumed the most sodium had a twenty-seven per cent higher risk of stroke. Previous studies had suggested a smaller effect, which the team attributes to better measurement. The national salt guideline, first introduced in nineteen ninety-eight, recommends no more than five grams of salt a day, a target that most adults still exceed.

Coastal geographers at a university in the Netherlands, directed by Professor Ishikawa, I, S, H, I, K, A, W, A, say that sea levels along the Dutch coast have risen by twenty-three centimetres since nineteen fifty, faster than most earlier projections. Using tide gauge records and altimetry data, the team calculates that the rate has accelerated by forty per cent over the past two decades. Earlier models had assumed a steady rise, but the authors warn that flood defences designed for twenty one hundred may need to be raised sooner.

Food scientists at a university in Belgium, supervised by Dr Lemarchand, L, E, M, A, R, C, H, A, N, D, compared the output of insect protein with that of beef. A kilogram of cricket protein requires about one thousand five hundred litres of water, compared with roughly fifteen thousand litres for beef. Insect farms also emit less methane, although earlier estimates had overstated the energy savings. In blind taste tests, thirty-eight per cent of volunteers could not tell the ground insect product from a standard meat patty.
